Variator (20) and forward clutch (Fwd/C) disposed in series are provided between engine (1) having starter motor (15) and driving wheel (7). Sailing stop control that, on the basis of satisfaction of sailing entering condition, interrupts power transmission by frictional engagement element (Fwd/C), stops engine (1) and performs coast-travel is performed. When sailing entering condition is satisfied, coast-travel is started with rotation stop timing of variator (20) being delayed with respect to rotation stop timing of engine (1). When accelerator pedal depression operation intervenes after start of coast-travel, engine (1) is restarted by starter motor (15). When judged that input and output rotation speeds of frictional engagement element (Fwd/C) become synchronization rotation speed after restart of engine (1), frictional engagement element (Fwd/C) is reengaged. Shift response from coast-travel to normal travel is therefore improved at change-of-mind at which sailing quitting condition is satisfied during progress of automatic stop of engine.

Keywords: Variator, Fwd, Sailing

outputs.L1: A variator (20) and a forward clutch (Fwd/C), arranged in series, are provided between an engine (1) equipped with a starter motor (15) and a driving wheel (7). Sailing stop control is performed when a sailing entry condition is satisfied; this control interrupts power transmission through the frictional engagement element (Fwd/C), stops the engine (1), and initiates coasting. When the sailing entry condition is satisfied, coasting begins while the rotation stop timing of the variator (20) is delayed relative to that of the engine (1). If the accelerator pedal is depressed after coasting has begun, the engine (1) is restarted by the starter motor (15). When it is determined that the input and output rotational speeds of the frictional engagement element (Fwd/C) have reached the synchronization rotational speed following the restart of the engine (1), the frictional engagement element (Fwd/C) is re-engaged. Consequently, the shift response from coasting to normal travel is improved in a change-of-mind situation in which a sailing exit condition is satisfied while the engine is being automatically stopped.
outputs.L2: A variator (20) and a forward clutch (Fwd/C), arranged in series, are installed between an engine (1) equipped with a starter motor (15) and a drive wheel (7). When a sailing-entry condition is met, sailing-stop control disengages the frictional engagement element (Fwd/C) to interrupt power transfer, shuts down the engine (1), and allows the vehicle to coast. At the beginning of coasting, rotation of the variator (20) is stopped later than rotation of the engine (1). If the accelerator pedal is depressed after coasting has commenced, the starter motor (15) restarts the engine (1). Once it is determined that the input and output rotational speeds of the frictional engagement element (Fwd/C) have reached a synchronized speed following the engine restart, the element (Fwd/C) is engaged again. Consequently, when a driver changes their intention and a sailing-exit condition arises while the engine is undergoing automatic shutdown, the transition from coasting to normal driving is made more responsive.
outputs.L3:
A variator and a forward clutch are arranged in series along the power transmission path between a starter-equipped engine and the vehicle’s driving wheel. When the conditions for entering a sailing mode are satisfied, the forward clutch disengages to interrupt power transmission, the engine is stopped, and the vehicle begins coasting. At the start of coast travel, the variator continues rotating temporarily, so its rotation stops later than that of the engine.

If the driver depresses the accelerator pedal while the vehicle is coasting, the starter motor restarts the engine. The forward clutch is then reengaged once the rotational speeds on its input and output sides have synchronized. This speed-matching control reduces engagement shock and provides a smoother transition from coasting back to normal powered driving.
outputs.L4:
A vehicle control system is configured to perform a sailing-stop operation when predetermined coasting conditions are satisfied, such as when the driver releases the accelerator pedal while the vehicle is traveling. During the sailing-stop operation, the controller disengages a forward clutch provided in the power-transmission path and automatically stops the engine. By disconnecting the engine from the drive wheels and eliminating fuel consumption during coasting, the system reduces power loss and improves fuel economy.

At the same time, the controller delays stoppage of a variator, such as the variable-speed mechanism of a continuously variable transmission. Maintaining rotation of the variator for a certain period after the engine has stopped preserves favorable transmission conditions and allows the transmission input side to respond more quickly if propulsion is requested. This delay may be achieved by controlling the timing of clutch disengagement, hydraulic pressure, or another transmission-related actuator so that the variator does not immediately come to rest.

If the driver depresses the accelerator pedal during the sailing-stop operation, the controller determines that a return to normal driving is required and initiates an engine restart. The engine speed and the rotational speed on the transmission side are then brought toward synchronization. The forward clutch is maintained in a disengaged or partially engaged state until the difference between the relevant rotational speeds has decreased to an acceptable level. Once synchronization is achieved, the controller reengages the forward clutch and restores torque transmission from the engine to the drive wheels.

Because rotation of the variator is prevented from stopping too early, less time is required to establish suitable transmission operating conditions after an acceleration request. Coordinating the engine restart, rotational synchronization, and clutch engagement also reduces engagement shock and suppresses abrupt changes in drive torque. The system therefore provides a quicker and smoother transition from fuel-saving sailing-stop coasting to powered driving when the driver requests acceleration during automatic engine shutdown.
outputs.L5:
## Variator, FWD, and Sailing: Technologies for Efficient Driving

Modern vehicles use several technologies to improve comfort, efficiency, and driving performance. Three terms commonly encountered are **variator**, **FWD**, and **sailing**.

A **variator**, also known as a continuously variable transmission (CVT), changes the transmission ratio smoothly rather than using fixed gears. This allows the engine to operate at an efficient speed while providing seamless acceleration. Variators are especially popular in compact cars, hybrids, scooters, and other vehicles designed for comfortable, economical travel.

**FWD**, or front-wheel drive, means that the engine sends power to the front wheels. This configuration is widely used because it is compact, cost-effective, and offers reliable traction in everyday conditions. Combining FWD with a variator can create a practical drivetrain that is easy to operate and well suited to urban driving.

The **sailing** function, sometimes called coasting, helps reduce fuel consumption. When the driver releases the accelerator under suitable conditions, the vehicle may disconnect the engine from the drivetrain or reduce engine braking. As a result, the car continues moving with minimal resistance, much like a sailing boat using its momentum. Some modern systems can also switch off the engine temporarily while coasting.

Together, a variator, FWD, and sailing technology can provide smooth acceleration, predictable handling, and improved energy efficiency. Their effectiveness, however, depends on vehicle design, road conditions, and driving style.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize a vehicle powertrain control invention that improves response when a driver presses the accelerator during sailing-stop operation.
counterfactuals.output:
The invention concerns a vehicle that, during **sailing-stop operation**, shuts off the engine and disconnects or reduces power transmission while the vehicle coasts. If the driver presses the accelerator in this state, conventional systems may respond slowly because the engine must first restart and the drivetrain must reconnect.

The proposed controller improves response by promptly:

1. Detecting the accelerator request during sailing-stop;
2. Cancelling sailing-stop and initiating engine restart;
3. Preparing the transmission or power-engagement element for the required driving force; and
4. Coordinating engine torque, rotational-speed matching, gear selection, and clutch engagement.

This coordinated control allows propulsion torque to reach the wheels sooner while limiting engagement shock or excessive engine-speed changes. The result is faster, smoother acceleration that better matches the driver’s intent after coasting with the engine stopped.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a patent-style abstract describing an engine, starter motor, variator, forward clutch, sailing stop control, and clutch reengagement after engine restart.
counterfactuals.output: A vehicle powertrain system includes an internal combustion engine, a starter motor configured to restart the engine, a variator configured to provide a continuously variable transmission ratio, and a forward clutch selectively coupling the engine to a drive wheel. A controller performs a sailing stop control in which the forward clutch is disengaged and the engine is stopped while the vehicle is traveling. In response to a request to terminate the sailing stop control, the controller operates the starter motor to restart the engine, controls the variator to establish a target transmission ratio, and thereafter reengages the forward clutch. During reengagement, the controller regulates clutch engagement pressure based on at least one of engine speed, variator input speed, vehicle speed, and requested drive torque so as to reduce rotational speed difference across the forward clutch. The system thereby suppresses engagement shock and limits clutch slip while promptly restoring driving force after engine restart.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain how delaying the variator’s rotation stop relative to the engine’s rotation stop can improve the transition from coasting back to normal driving.
counterfactuals.output:
When coasting, the engine may be shut down or disconnected to save fuel. If the variator is allowed to keep rotating briefly after the engine stops, it retains rotational energy, lubrication pressure, and—depending on the design—can move toward a suitable transmission ratio.

When normal driving resumes:

- the variator is not restarting from a completely stationary, high-friction condition;
- its ratio and speed can be matched more quickly to the engine and vehicle;
- belts, pulleys, clutches, or other transmission elements take up torque more gradually; and
- the engine sees less sudden load during restart or reconnection.

The result is faster torque recovery with less hesitation, shock, vibration, or driveline “jerk.” In short, delaying the variator’s stop creates a smoother bridge between engine-off coasting and powered driving.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a concise technical summary of a control method in which an engine is automatically stopped during coast travel and restarted when accelerator operation intervenes, with the forward clutch engaged after rotational synchronization.
counterfactuals.output: A vehicle control method stops the engine automatically during coasting while the forward clutch is disengaged. When accelerator operation is detected, the engine is restarted and its rotational speed is synchronized with the transmission input speed. After synchronization is achieved, the forward clutch is engaged to resume propulsion smoothly and suppress engagement shock.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4
